title: Concentration Inequalities and Limit Theorems
description: Markov, Chebyshev and Hoeffding inequalities, the law of large numbers, the central limit theorem and Monte Carlo estimation.
overview: Why does averaging many noisy measurements give a reliable answer? Why do test-set errors get close to true errors as the test set grows, and why do so many quantities look Gaussian? The answers are the limit theorems of probability. They are the reason that statistics and machine learning work at all: they turn the randomness of individual examples into predictable behavior of averages.

This chapter proves the basic tail inequalities, states the law of large numbers and the central limit theorem, and shows how they quantify the error of an average. These results are used constantly in the Machine Learning book, in the generalization bounds of learning theory and in the inference of the Data Science book.
objectives: State and apply Markov's and Chebyshev's inequalities, and Hoeffding's inequality for bounded variables.
State the law of large numbers and derive the sample size needed for a given accuracy.
State the central limit theorem, and use it to approximate the distribution of sums and binomial counts.
Quantify the error of Monte Carlo estimates and of an empirical average, and explain the 1/√n rate.
Recognize when the theorems fail, for example with infinite variance.

sections.title: Tail bounds: Markov, Chebyshev and Hoeffding
body: Suppose the average height in a room is 170 cm. Could a randomly chosen person be 340 cm? Not likely, because heights cannot be that far above the average for many people at once: if even a tenth of people were that tall, the average would be pushed well above 170. Tail bounds turn this common sense into numbers. They say that a variable cannot often be far from its mean, using only a little knowledge of its distribution. How likely is a random variable to be far from its mean? Without knowing the distribution, simple bounds still hold.

body.key: Markov's inequality. If X ≥ 0 and t > 0, then P(X ≥ t) ≤ E[X]/t.

body: **Proof.** E[X] ≥ E[X · 1{X ≥ t}] ≥ t · P(X ≥ t), since on the event X ≥ t the variable is at least t. ∎ For example, a non-negative quantity with mean 10 exceeds 50 with probability at most 10/50 = 0.2.
Applying Markov to the non-negative variable (X − μ)² gives **Chebyshev's inequality**:

body.eq: P( |X − μ| ≥ t ) ≤ σ²/t²,    P( |X − μ| ≥ kσ ) ≤ 1/k²

body: At least 89% of any distribution lies within three standard deviations of its mean (1 − 1/9). The bound is loose for specific distributions (a Gaussian has 99.7% within 3σ) but holds for all distributions with finite variance.
When the variables are bounded and independent, tails decay exponentially fast, not only polynomially. If X₁, …, X_n are independent with X_i ∈ [a_i, b_i] and X̄ is their mean, then

body.eq: P( | X̄ − E[X̄] | ≥ t ) ≤ 2 exp( −2n²t² / Σ_i (b_i − a_i)² )

body: For variables in [0, 1] this is 2e^{−2nt²}. This is the inequality used in learning theory to show that the training error is close to the true error.

example.title: Chebyshev versus Hoeffding
example.problem: An average of n = 1000 independent Bernoulli(0.5) variables. Bound P(|X̄ − 0.5| ≥ 0.05) with Chebyshev and with Hoeffding.
example.solution: Var(X̄) = 0.25/1000 = 0.00025. Chebyshev: 0.00025/0.05² = 0.1. Hoeffding: 2e^{−2(1000)(0.0025)} = 2e^{−5} = 0.0135. The exponential bound is about 7 times smaller, and the gap grows with n.

body.note: The Chernoff method behind Hoeffding applies Markov's inequality to e^{sX} and optimizes over s. A variable is sub-Gaussian if its tails are at least as light as a Gaussian's; bounded variables and Gaussians are. The learning-theory chapter uses these bounds together with the union bound.

sections.title: The law of large numbers
body: Flip a fair coin 10 times and you might get 7 heads (70%). Flip it 10,000 times and the fraction of heads will be very close to 50%. The more you average, the more the random ups and downs cancel, and what is left is the true underlying rate. That is the law of large numbers. Let X₁, X₂, … be independent and identically distributed with mean μ and variance σ², and let X̄_n be the average of the first n. The **law of large numbers** says that the sample mean converges to the true mean as n grows.

list: **Weak law**: X̄_n → μ **in probability**: for every ε > 0, P(|X̄_n − μ| > ε) → 0.
**Strong law**: X̄_n → μ **almost surely**: with probability one, the sequence of averages converges to μ.

body: The weak law follows at once from Chebyshev's inequality, since E[X̄_n] = μ and Var(X̄_n) = σ²/n:

The same calculation gives a sample size: to get within ε of μ with probability at least 1 − δ it suffices that n ≥ σ²/(ε²δ). Hoeffding for bounded variables gives the much better n ≥ ln(2/δ)/(2ε²) (for variables in [0, 1]).

example.title: How many coin flips?
example.problem: Estimate the heads probability p of a coin to within 0.05 with confidence 95%. Compare the sample sizes guaranteed by Chebyshev (using σ² ≤ 1/4) and Hoeffding.
example.solution: Chebyshev: n ≥ 0.25/(0.0025 × 0.05) = 2000. Hoeffding: n ≥ ln(40)/(2 × 0.0025) = 3.689/0.005 = 738. The exponential bound needs 2.7 times fewer flips. (The CLT, below, gives about 385.)

body: The law of large numbers justifies **Monte Carlo** methods: to estimate an expectation E[g(X)], average g over random samples. The error shrinks like σ/√n whatever the dimension of X, which is why Monte Carlo is the tool for high-dimensional integrals (Bayesian posteriors, reinforcement learning returns, partition functions).

example.title: Estimating π
example.problem: Throw n random points into the unit square and count the fraction p̂ inside the quarter circle (probability π/4). How accurate is 4p̂ for n = 10⁶?
example.solution: The standard error of p̂ is √(p(1 − p)/n) with p = 0.785: √(0.1686/10⁶) = 4.1 × 10⁻⁴. Multiply by 4 for the estimate of π: standard error 0.0016. To gain one more digit of accuracy requires 100 times more points: the 1/√n rate.

body: Each average of a loss over a mini-batch, each test-set accuracy and each sample estimate of an expectation in this library is justified by this theorem. It says what the answer converges to, but not how fast: that is the job of the next section.

sections.title: The central limit theorem
body: The law of large numbers says where the average ends up. The CLT says what the leftover error looks like: the shape of the scatter of averages around μ. Take any distribution at all, lopsided or flat or lumpy, draw many samples and average them, and repeat this many times. A histogram of those averages will look like a bell curve, narrower the more samples each average uses. The **central limit theorem** (CLT) describes the fluctuations around μ.

body.key: Central limit theorem. If X₁, …, X_n are i.i.d. with mean μ and finite variance σ², then the standardized average √n (X̄_n − μ)/σ converges in distribution to the standard normal N(0, 1) as n → ∞. So for large n, X̄_n ≈ N(μ, σ²/n) and the sum ΣX_i ≈ N(nμ, nσ²).

body: The shape of the distribution of the individual X_i does not matter: whether the variables are coin flips, dice or exponentials, averages become bell-shaped. This is why the Gaussian is the default model of noise, which is a sum of many small independent effects.

example.title: A binomial count
example.problem: A fair coin is flipped 100 times. Estimate the probability of at least 60 heads.
example.solution: The number of heads is Binomial(100, 0.5), with mean 50 and standard deviation √(100 × 0.25) = 5. Use the continuity correction (a discrete value k occupies the interval k ± 0.5): P(X ≥ 60) = P(X ≥ 59.5) ≈ P(Z ≥ (59.5 − 50)/5) = P(Z ≥ 1.9) = 0.0287. The exact binomial value is 0.0284.

example.title: Sum of dice
example.solution: One die has mean 3.5 and variance 35/12. The sum has mean 350 and variance 100 × 35/12 = 291.7, so standard deviation 17.08. P(sum ≥ 381) ≈ P(Z ≥ (380.5 − 350)/17.08) = P(Z ≥ 1.79) = 0.037.

body.h: Confidence intervals and the standard error

body: Because X̄ ≈ N(μ, σ²/n), the interval X̄ ± 1.96σ/√n captures μ with probability about 95%. The quantity σ/√n is the **standard error** (estimated with the sample standard deviation s). This gives the confidence interval for an accuracy used in Evaluating Models, with σ² = p(1 − p): for the coin-flip problem above, ε = 0.05 requires 1.96 × 0.5/√n ≤ 0.05, i.e. n ≥ 385.

list: It needs **finite variance**. The Cauchy distribution (heavy tailed) has no mean; the average of n Cauchy samples has the same distribution as a single one, and does not concentrate at all. Financial returns and network traffic with heavy tails converge slowly or not in the CLT sense.
It is asymptotic: the **Berry–Esseen** theorem bounds the error of the normal approximation by about C·ρ/(σ³√n), so skewed distributions need larger n.
It needs independence (or weak dependence). Strongly correlated data, such as time series with long memory, have a slower convergence and a larger effective variance.

sections.title: Where these results appear in machine learning
terms: central limit theorem in machine learning

list: **Test and validation error**: the accuracy on m held-out examples is an average of Bernoulli variables. Hoeffding gives the generalization guarantee of the learning theory chapter, and the CLT gives its confidence interval p̂ ± 1.96√(p̂(1 − p̂)/m).

**Mini-batch gradients**: a mini-batch of size b averages b per-example gradients. By the CLT the noise has covariance about Σ/b, so a batch four times larger halves the noise: the scaling behind the learning rate and batch size rules of Training Deep Networks.
**Ensembles**: averaging B models reduces variance as σ²/B only if their errors are independent; correlation ρ leaves a floor ρσ² (see Ensembles).
**The bootstrap and confidence intervals** rely on the same approximate normality of estimators (see Estimation and Bootstrap in the Data Science book).
**Monte Carlo** is used for Bayesian posteriors (MCMC), expectations in reinforcement learning, and approximating normalizing constants.

**Initialization**: the sum of n independent terms in a neuron's pre-activation is approximately Gaussian by the CLT, with variance n·Var(w)E[x²]; this is the reasoning behind Xavier and He initialization.

example.title: Noise in a mini-batch gradient
example.problem: A per-example gradient component has standard deviation 2. What is the standard deviation of the average over a mini-batch of 64, and of 256?
example.solution: 2/√64 = 0.25 and 2/√256 = 0.125. Quadrupling the batch size halves the gradient noise, with diminishing returns for the cost of 4 times the computation.

quiz.q: A non-negative quantity has mean 8. What does Markov's inequality say about P(X ≥ 40)?
quiz.why: P(X ≥ t) ≤ E[X]/t = 8/40 = 0.2. Markov gives only an upper bound, and the actual probability may be far smaller.

quiz.q: A variable has mean 100 and standard deviation 5, with an unknown distribution. Which bound on P(|X − 100| ≥ 15) is guaranteed?
quiz.why: 15 is k = 3 standard deviations, so Chebyshev gives 1/k² = 1/9. The Gaussian figure 0.0027 is not guaranteed for a general distribution, and 1/3 uses 1/k instead of 1/k².

quiz.q: For the average of n independent bounded variables, how do the Chebyshev and Hoeffding bounds on a deviation behave as n grows?
quiz.a: Chebyshev decays like 1/n, and Hoeffding decays exponentially in n
wrong: Chebyshev decays exponentially in n, and Hoeffding decays like 1/n
Chebyshev decays like 1/n², and Hoeffding like 1/n
quiz.why: Chebyshev uses only the variance σ²/n, giving a 1/n rate. Boundedness lets Hoeffding exploit the exponential moment, so the tail falls like e^{−2nt²}.

quiz.q: n = 200 independent variables lie in [0, 1]. What is Hoeffding's bound on P(|X̄ − E[X̄]| ≥ 0.1)?
quiz.why: The bound is 2e^{−2nt²} = 2e^{−2(200)(0.01)} = 2e⁻⁴. Dropping the factor 2 (which covers both tails) gives 0.018.

quiz.q: Chebyshev guarantees accuracy ε with probability 1 − δ when n ≥ σ²/(ε²δ). With σ² = 1, ε = 0.1 and δ = 0.05, how many samples suffice?
quiz.why: n ≥ 1/(0.01 × 0.05) = 2000. Using ε instead of ε² gives 200, and dropping δ gives 100.

quiz.q: After 1,000 fair-coin flips there are 40 more heads than tails. What does the law of large numbers imply about later flips?
quiz.a: They are unaffected; the heads fraction still tends to 0.5 because the early excess is diluted
wrong: Tails become more likely until the counts even out
The excess of heads must also tend to 0, so later flips favor tails
The law says nothing about the heads fraction for a finite number of flips
quiz.why: The law concerns the fraction X̄_n, which converges to 0.5. The raw difference between heads and tails does not need to return to 0, and the coin has no memory.

quiz.q: A Monte Carlo estimate with 10,000 samples has standard error 0.02. About how many samples are needed for a standard error of 0.005?
quiz.why: The error falls as 1/√n, so cutting it by a factor of 4 needs 4² = 16 times as many samples. A factor of 4 in samples only halves the error.

quiz.q: Why is Monte Carlo the standard tool for high-dimensional expectations?
quiz.a: Its error behaves like σ/√n whatever the dimension of X
wrong: Its error falls like 1/n regardless of the dimension
It evaluates the integrand at fewer points than any grid method in every dimension
It is exact whenever the integrand is smooth
quiz.why: The law of large numbers and the standard error σ/√n do not involve the dimension, whereas grids need exponentially many points. The 1/√n rate is slow but dimension-free.

quiz.q: The sum of 64 i.i.d. variables, each with mean 2 and variance 4, is used. What is the approximate probability that the sum exceeds 140?
quiz.why: The sum has mean 128 and variance 256, so sd 16, and z = 12/16 = 0.75. P(Z > 0.75) ≈ 0.227; the value 0.773 is the probability of falling below.

quiz.q: X ~ Binomial(100, 0.3). With a continuity correction, the normal approximation to P(X ≤ 24) is Φ of
quiz.why: The mean is 30 and the variance is 100(0.3)(0.7) = 21. The event X ≤ 24 covers the interval up to 24.5, and the denominator is the standard deviation √21, not the variance.

quiz.q: What is the distribution of the average of 1,000 independent standard Cauchy samples?
quiz.a: The same standard Cauchy as a single sample, so averaging does not concentrate it
wrong: Approximately normal with standard deviation about 1/√1000
A Cauchy distribution about 1000 times narrower
Approximately normal, but with heavier tails than usual
quiz.why: The Cauchy has no mean or finite variance, so neither the law of large numbers nor the CLT applies. The sample average is distributed exactly as one observation.

quiz.q: A sensor logs 100,000 readings, each repeating the previous one with probability 0.99. Why does the standard error σ/√100000 understate the uncertainty in the mean?
quiz.a: The readings are strongly dependent, so the effective sample size is far below 100,000
wrong: The σ/√n formula is valid only for n below 10,000
Repeated values make the variance infinite
The CLT requires the readings to be bounded
quiz.why: The σ/√n rate assumes independent (or weakly dependent) observations. With long runs of near-identical readings there is much less information than the count suggests.

quiz.q: A classifier is right on 360 of 400 independent test examples. Which 95% confidence interval for its accuracy does the CLT give?
quiz.why: SE = √(0.9 × 0.1/400) = 0.015, and the interval is 1.96 SE = 0.029. The value 0.015 is one standard error without the factor 1.96.

quiz.q: A poll wants a 95% margin of error of 0.03 for a proportion near 0.5. Using the CLT, about how many respondents are needed?
quiz.why: Solve 1.96 × 0.5/√n ≤ 0.03: √n ≥ 32.7, so n ≥ 1,067. The figure 385 corresponds to a margin of 0.05.

quiz.q: Which distribution would need the largest n before the normal approximation to its sample mean is accurate?
quiz.a: A highly skewed distribution with rare large values
wrong: A symmetric distribution such as the uniform
quiz.why: The Berry–Esseen error is governed by the third moment relative to σ³ and falls as 1/√n, so skew slows convergence. Gaussians are exactly normal for every n.

quiz.q: A mini-batch of 32 examples gives a gradient with noise standard deviation 0.5. What batch size gives noise standard deviation 0.1?
quiz.why: Noise falls as 1/√b, so a fivefold reduction needs 5² = 25 times the batch: 25 × 32 = 800. A factor of 5 in batch size (160) reduces noise only by about 2.2.

quiz.q: Fifty models each have error variance 4, with pairwise error correlation 0.5. As more such models are averaged, the variance of the average approaches
quiz.why: The variance of the average is ρσ² + (1 − ρ)σ²/B, which tends to the floor ρσ² = 2. The formula σ²/B applies only to independent errors.

quiz.q: A neuron's pre-activation sums 256 independent terms w_i x_i, with Var(w) = 0.01 and E[x²] = 1. What is the variance of the sum?
quiz.why: Variances of independent terms add: 256 × 0.01 × 1 = 2.56. The value 1.6 is the standard deviation, and by the CLT the sum is approximately Gaussian.

summary: Markov: P(X ≥ t) ≤ E[X]/t for X ≥ 0. Chebyshev: P(|X − μ| ≥ kσ) ≤ 1/k². Hoeffding gives exponentially small tails for bounded independent variables: P(|X̄ − μ| ≥ t) ≤ 2e^{−2nt²} on [0, 1].
The law of large numbers: the sample mean converges to μ (weakly in probability by Chebyshev, strongly almost surely). Its standard error is σ/√n.

The CLT: √n(X̄ − μ)/σ → N(0, 1) for i.i.d. variables with finite variance. Use it to approximate sums and binomial counts (with a continuity correction) and to form confidence intervals X̄ ± 1.96σ/√n.
Monte Carlo errors scale as 1/√n regardless of dimension. Halving the error costs four times the samples.
The CLT fails for heavy tails with infinite variance. These theorems underpin test-set evaluation, mini-batch SGD, ensembles, bootstrap and initialization.

problems.q: A random variable has mean 20 and standard deviation 4. Use Chebyshev to bound P(|X − 20| ≥ 10), and Markov to bound P(X ≥ 60) if X ≥ 0.
A model's error rate is estimated on m = 2500 test examples as 0.08. Give a 95% confidence interval using the CLT, and the Hoeffding half-width for the same confidence.
problems.solution: CLT: SE = √(0.08 × 0.92/2500) = 0.0054, so the interval is 0.08 ± 0.0106. Hoeffding: √(ln(40)/(2 × 2500)) = √(3.689/5000) = 0.0272. The CLT interval is narrower because it uses the actual variance (small for p near 0), while Hoeffding allows the worst case.

problems.q: Each of 36 independent measurements has standard deviation 3. How large is the standard error of their mean, and the probability that the mean is off by more than 1?
A fair coin is flipped 400 times. Find the probability that the number of heads is between 190 and 210 inclusive.
problems.solution: Mean 200, standard deviation √(400 × 0.25) = 10. With continuity correction, P(189.5 ≤ X ≤ 210.5) ≈ P(−1.05 ≤ Z ≤ 1.05) = 2(0.8531) − 1 = 0.706.

problems.q: To estimate an integral by Monte Carlo with a standard error of 0.001 when one sample has standard deviation 2, how many samples are needed?
